name: Gabon
sources: GDP $5.95bn: World Bank NY.GDP.MKTP.CD, series GAB, 1990 = 5,952,294,000. Against a population of 949,493 that is $6,269 a head - SIX times Cameroon's, twenty-one times Chad's, and higher than Portugal's was a decade earlier. Gabon is the richest state per head in this roster's Africa and one of the most unequal on earth, and both halves of that sentence come out of the same 270,000 barrels a day.

Population 0.95m: World Bank SP.POP.TOTL, series GAB, 1990 = 949,493. Under a million people in a country the size of the United Kingdom, which is the fact behind everything else here: Gabon's labour force was so small that the timber camps and the Moanda manganese mine ran on migrant workers from Cameroon, Equatorial Guinea and Mali, and Libreville expelled them by the tens of thousands whenever politics required it.

TFP trend 0.0: real GDP grew 5.19% in 1990 (World Bank NY.GDP.MKTP.KD.ZG, series GAB), and none of that is productivity. It is the Rabi-Kounga field, found in 1985 and brought on stream in 1989, which took national production from 208,000 barrels a day in 1989 to 270,000 in 1990 and 294,000 in 1991, arriving in the same year Iraq's invasion of Kuwait put $20 on the price. A pure rentier's total factor productivity is the wrong question and 0.0 is the honest answer to it: nothing in Gabonese output outside the oil sector was getting more efficient, and nothing was collapsing either. Entered at zero rather than negative for that reason, and it is the only zero in this region.

Inflation 7.73%: World Bank FP.CPI.TOTL.ZG, series GAB, 1990 = 7.7253%. THE HIGHEST IN THE FRANC ZONE by a wide margin - six times Cameroon's 1.1%, in a currency union whose whole point is that its members cannot have their own inflation. The reason is that Gabon in 1990 was an oil boom inside a fixed peg with a non-tradable sector that could not expand: prices in Libreville were famously the highest in Africa. The IMF's WEO puts the same year at 15.4%, roughly double, and the divergence is worth flagging - the consumer-price series is entered because every other file in this roster uses it, and the disagreement is a fair warning that neither figure is well measured.

Interest rate 11%: NOT A GABONESE NUMBER. The Banque des Etats de l'Afrique Centrale taux d'escompte, as in chad.json and the other three BEAC files. FR.INR.LEND has no Gabonese entry for 1990. The loader's coupled check reads 0.025 - (0.11 - 0.0773) = -0.008, the tightest real rate of the six and the only one anywhere near neutral, which is a coincidence of Gabon's inflation being high rather than of anyone in Libreville choosing it.

Revenue 30% of GDP: NOT SOURCED, and the largest bracket in this file. GC.REV.XGRT.GD.ZS has no Gabonese entry for 1990. 0.30 is set well above Cameroon's sourced 14.26% because Gabonese central government revenue in this period was oil royalties and the profit tax on Elf Gabon and Shell Gabon, which the IMF's Article IV reporting of the era put around 30% of GDP at 1990 prices. Read it as a bracket, and read it alongside the debt figure below: a state taking 30% of a large output and still owing 75% of it.

Military 2.5% of GDP: NOT SOURCED - MS.MIL.XPND.GD.ZS has no Gabonese entry for any year of the 1990s. 0.025 is entered as a bracket above Chad's sourced 1.98% and the Central African Republic's 1.6% and well below Congo's 4.2%. The justification is composition rather than a number: Gabon had only about 4,000 men under arms but bought as if it had far more - Mirage 5s, a Combattante missile boat, and a Garde Presidentielle better equipped than the army - and it did so out of an oil budget. A reader checking this file should treat this line as unverified.

Investment 7.5% public and 14.2% private: gross capital formation was 21.68% of GDP (World Bank NE.GDI.TOTL.ZS, series GAB, 1990 = 21.6772), the highest in this region and half again Congo's. The 7.5/14.2 split is APPORTIONED and sums to the sourced total; weighted private because the capital going in was Elf's and Shell's at Rabi-Kounga.

Debt 75% of GDP: World Bank DT.DOD.DECT.GN.ZS, series GAB, 1990 = 74.6368, external debt stocks as a share of GNI. High for a rich country and it is the Transgabonais - the 670 km railway from Owendo to Franceville, begun in 1974 on the strength of $12 oil and finished in 1986 after it had gone to $9, which cost something like $4bn and is most of this number. Gabon was rescheduling at the Paris Club in 1987, 1988, 1989, 1991 and 1994.

Oil 0.270 mbd: 270,000 barrels a day in 1990 (US EIA international series; 208,000 in 1989, 294,000 in 1991, peaking near 365,000 in 1996-97). The third-largest producer in this roster's Africa after Nigeria and Angola. Gabon was an OPEC member from 1975 until it left on 1 January 1995 - it is the only OPEC member in this roster besides the Gulf states, Nigeria, Algeria, Libya, Iran, Iraq and Venezuela, and it left because the membership fee had come to cost more than the quota was worth.

Stability 42 and authoritarianism 0.78: Omar Bongo had been president since December 1967 and the Parti Democratique Gabonais the sole legal party since March 1968. Stability 42 is set above Congo's 35 and just above Chad's, and below the Central African Republic's 40 is where it would sit on the January facts alone - but it is put at 42 rather than 50 because Gabon in the first days of 1990 was already coming apart in a way Bangui was not. Strikes by students and then by the whole public sector ran through January and February; Bongo convened the Rendez-vous de Mars conference from 23 March, which voted itself into a constitutional convention; the opposition leader Joseph Rendjambe was found dead in a Libreville hotel on 23 May; Port-Gentil rose, Elf's installations were seized, and France sent 500 paratroopers under Operation Requin. All of that is inside the game's first year and NONE of it is scheduled here. Authoritarianism 0.78 sits just below Cameroon's 0.80: a sole legal party, but one with an unusually open patronage system and a president who negotiated rather than shot.

Separatism 0.05: the lowest in this region, level with Italy's. Gabon is forty-odd small ethnic groups with no majority - the Fang are about a third - and none of them has ever asked for a border. What Gabon has instead of separatism is a regional politics of who gets the oil rent, which is a different mechanism and lives in the government table.

Military strength 0.9: about 4,000 men in the Forces Armees Gabonaises, plus a Garde Presidentielle of 1,500 that was deliberately the better force, and behind both of them the French 6th Battalion d'Infanterie de Marine garrisoned at Libreville under the accord of 17 August 1960. That garrison put Leon Mba back in power against his own army in February 1964 and covered the evacuation at Port-Gentil in 1990. Set below Cameroon's 1.5 and above the Central African Republic's 0.6, which puts a well-equipped force of four thousand in the right place; the number that actually deterred anything in Libreville belongs to France.

pop_growth_1990 = 2.8049%/yr. Compound annual growth of World Bank SP.POP.TOTL, series GAB (Gabon): 833,501 in 1984 to 957,138 in 1989 — the five years ending on the eve of the 1 January 1990 start date. See EconomyRecord::pop_growth_1990 in spheres-sim/src/data/mod.rs for why the window ends in 1989 and not with the single-year 1990 rate.

note: 1990 TECHNOLOGY: AUTHORED, NOT DERIVED. What this nation knew on 1 January 1990 is transcribed and sourced grant by grant, exactly like every other 1990 figure in this file, and is not read off tfp_trend - there was never a code path from the trend to the known set, and the zero that stood there was a claim about the world rather than an absence of one (BIBLE section 8 and iron rule 4, both amended 2026-08-30). THE PREDICATE IS SPLIT, and split by the technology's OWN EFFECT TYPE so that it is mechanically computable and never a per-nation judgement call. A node whose effects include MilitaryEfficiency, MilitaryStrength, DiffusionEmission or CostReduction is SOVEREIGNTY-SIDE: holding it means this nation could PRODUCE it, so operating an imported article does not qualify. Every other node is USE-SIDE: deployed and in operational use here is enough, whoever built it, because the effect such a node pays is a productivity, health or output effect and that effect is real in the country where the machine runs. Of the 48 technologies the tree lets anyone hold in 1990, 17 are sovereignty-side and 31 are use-side.

DATA-KEYED TAIL NATION. This nation is outside the 29 authored majors, so nothing here was authored technology by technology: a grant is made only where one of two named published global series supports it, and nothing is modelled, estimated or interpolated. A short list, or an empty one, is the correct outcome of that rule and not a gap in the work.

Data-keyed tail nation: not one of the 29 authored majors. Only the two series named in ruling 3 were consulted - WHO/UNICEF WUENIC DTP3 1990 and World Bank IT.CEL.SETS. Nothing was modelled, estimated or interpolated, and no other evidence was admitted. ISO3 key used for both series: GAB.
AUTHORED, AND THE ANSWER IS NOTHING. Both named series were checked and both refused this nation; the empty grant list is a finding, not an absence of work.
